title: Jellyfish: Even Cooler than Octopi?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore jellyfish and comb jellies, covering how they are built (mesoglea, nerve nets, single body opening), the differences between true jellies (Scyphozoa, Cubozoa, Hydrozoa, Staurozoa) and comb jellies (Ctenophora) including locomotion with cilia versus bell pulsing, the debate over their relatedness, fossils dating back about five million years, feeding and stinging cells (nematocysts and colloblasts), dangerous species like the box jellyfish and irukandji, reproduction and life cycles including polyps and immortal Turritopsis, jellyfish blooms and their causes such as overfishing, nutrient runoff, climate change and ocean sprawl, and the Black Sea sea walnut invasion. The episode ends with listener mail from Stephen Hall about his wedding and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about mornings, fondue pots, and their enthusiasm for jellyfish as a sea creature compared with octopus.

segments.title: Jellyfish versus comb jellies
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the two groups, noting they look alike but genetics suggests they may not be closely related, and that scientists debate how closely they are related.

segments.title: Body structure and nervous system
segments.summary: Both groups have an outer epidermis, inner gastrodermis, and a jelly-like mesoglea that is mostly seawater. They have one body opening serving as mouth and anus, absorb nutrients through the skin, and have a nerve net. Box jellyfish have eyes with lenses and retinas but no brain, which puzzles scientists.

segments.title: Comb jelly locomotion and jellyfish polyps
segments.summary: Comb jellies swim using eight rows of cilia that scatter light to look rainbow-colored, and use sticky colloblast tentacles rather than stinging cells. Jellyfish have a medusa adult form and a polyp juvenile form that can resemble a plant.

segments.title: Types of jellyfish and Portuguese man of war
segments.summary: Scyphozoa are the most common true jellyfish, Hydrozoa often spend time as polyps and include colonial siphonophores like the Portuguese man of war, a colony of genetically identical individuals. Cubozoa are the box jellyfish with the most potent venom. Staurozoa are stalked jellies that cling to things. A freshwater jellyfish lives in the Great Lakes, likely introduced from China.

segments.title: Jellyfish movement and comb jelly diversity
segments.summary: Jellyfish move by contracting their bells, which creates vortices that help propel them using less energy. The hosts then cover comb jelly groups: cydippids with branching tentacles that can be retracted, lobed forms, and beroids that have no tentacles and use cilia-lined mouths to pull prey apart.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with banter about a pelican eating a pigeon video.

segments.title: Evolution, fossils, and feeding
segments.summary: Comb jellies and jellyfish have no hard parts yet a five-million-year-old jellyfish fossil was found in Utah. Scientists think comb jellies may have branched off very early in animal evolution. Both groups are carnivores; jellyfish are eaten by fish, sea turtles and sunfish, and are eaten by people in parts of Asia, and a fishery exists in Georgia.

segments.title: Stings, nematocysts, and Irukandji syndrome
segments.summary: Jellyfish nematocysts fire venom-bearing harpoons within a fraction of a second. The sea wasp has the most potent venom for humans. The tiny Irukandji causes severe symptoms including back pain, vomiting, and a sense of impending doom. Irukandji have been found off Florida and South Africa. The hosts discuss first aid: freshwater can trigger remaining nematocysts, so seawater rinsing and scraping with a credit card is advised.

segments.title: Comb jelly feeding and defense
segments.summary: Comb jellies capture prey with sticky glue on their tentacles and reel it to the mouth. One comb jelly species steals and reuses stinging cells from the jellies it eats. Jellies use bioluminescence and red pigment as defense.

segments.title: Reproduction, lifespan, and immortality
segments.summary: Jellyfish reproduce sexually in varied ways, with some hermaphroditic and some split-sex, and spawn eggs and sperm through the mouth. Polyps reproduce asexually by budding and strobilation. Turritopsis can revert from medusa to polyp, making it effectively immortal.

segments.title: Jellyfish blooms and human impacts
segments.summary: Jellyfish blooms can clog power plants, fisheries, and a US Navy warship's cooling system. Possible causes include overfishing, fertilizer runoff, climate change and warming waters, and ocean sprawl with artificial structures. The Black Sea invasion by sea walnuts collapsed fisheries until a predator jellyfish arrived.

segments.title: Listener mail: Stephen Hall wedding
segments.summary: Listener Stephen Hall thanks the hosts for podcast episodes that calmed him before his wedding.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and sign off.
